title: America Turns 250: Teddy Has Some Advice
author: Arthur Brooks
source: Arthur Brooks Newsletter / The Free Press
summary: Arthur Brooks delivers a speech written for the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, North Dakota — a meditation on Roosevelt's philosophy and its application to America on its 250th anniversary. Brooks traces Roosevelt's formative crisis: as a young man, TR lost both his mother and his wife on the same day in February 1884, a grief that drove him to the Badlands where he found in the landscape's austerity the philosophy he would carry for the rest of his life. That philosophy was the strenuous life: the conviction that suffering and struggle are not obstacles to a good life but constitutive of it — that comfort is the enemy of character, and that the hardships a person chooses to embrace define who they become. Brooks uses Roosevelt's story to argue that America's greatest strength has never been its comfort or abundance but its willingness to choose hard things. The speech closes with a call for contemporary Americans to recover this ethic: to build rather than consume, to choose difficulty over ease, and to resist the comfortable mediocrity that Roosevelt identified as democracy's deepest enemy.
points: Roosevelt's formative philosophy was born from catastrophic loss rather than from success: the double bereavement of February 14, 1884 drove him to the Badlands, where the demands of outdoor life and the austerity of the landscape forged the strenuous-life ethic he would teach for the rest of his career.

The strenuous life is a philosophical program, not an aesthetic preference: TR's argument was that voluntarily chosen difficulty builds the character that imposed hardship merely tests, and that the deliberate avoidance of struggle is the deliberate avoidance of growth.

Brooks uses Roosevelt's biography to argue that America's historical strength is the cultural willingness to choose hard things — a capacity he identifies as under threat from a contemporary premium on ease, comfort, and consumption.

The opening of the TR Presidential Library at Medora — the place where Roosevelt found himself — serves as a physical reminder that character is formed in adversity and that the landscapes and conditions we choose to inhabit shape who we become.

Brooks's civic argument scales personal philosophy to national life: a culture of people who embrace difficulty, build rather than consume, and pursue excellence over comfort is a culture capable of self-governance, and the converse is equally true.

Theodore Roosevelt is a near-mythical figure in American history. He is famous for his courage in the Spanish-American War, and his fortitude as president of the United States. (After an assassination attempt during his 1912 re-election effort, he went on to give a campaign speech with a bullet lodged in his chest.) He is admired, too, for the style—rarely seen in today’s brash, performative politics—that he derived from his favorite aphorism: “Speak softly and carry a big stick.” Teddy Roosevelt was a man with a clear philosophy of life, which he found as a young man in Medora, North Dakota.

He became a hero of the Spanish-American War, secretary of the U.S. Navy, governor of New York, vice president of the United States, and finally a two-term president.

Yet I strongly suspect that, on this 250th anniversary of our nation, Roosevelt himself would have had a grander ambition than individual self-improvement.
